By the middle of the 1400s, Sufi Muslims in Yemen were roasting and brewing the seeds of the coffee plant, which grows wild in the highlands of Ethiopia. This is the first reliable record of coffee as a drink. How and when the plant crossed the Red Sea is not known; the story of the Ethiopian goatherd Kaldi is a later legend.

Members of Sufi orders drank it to stay awake through night prayers. From Yemen, coffee drinking spread with traders and pilgrims:

  • to Mecca by about 1500, where the governor briefly banned it in 1511;
  • to Cairo and Damascus early in the 1500s;
  • to Istanbul, where the first coffeehouses opened in the 1550s.

Coffeehouses became places for talk, games, music and news, and rulers and religious scholars often tried to close them, without lasting success.

For two centuries Yemen grew nearly all the world's coffee. Ships loaded it at the port of Mocha, and the Mocha trade carried it to India, Egypt and Europe. The monopoly broke when the Dutch planted coffee in Java in 1696, and later when the French and Portuguese took it to the Americas, where Brazil became the largest grower.
